items.stem: Define the term "displacement (oscillation)".
items.answer: The distance and direction of the object from its equilibrium position
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the distance and direction of the object from its equilibrium position. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Briefly explain why the period of an SHM oscillator does not depend on the amplitude.
items.answer: In SHM a larger displacement gives a proportionally larger restoring acceleration; the object travels further but faster, and the time per cycle depends only on ω.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: In SHM a larger displacement gives a proportionally larger restoring acceleration; the object travels further but faster, and the time per cycle depends only on ω. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Arjun writes: "All oscillations are simple harmonic." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Only oscillations with a ∝ −x are SHM; a bouncing ball or large-angle pendulum is periodic but not SHM.
items.markingKey: Only oscillations with a ∝ −x are SHM; a bouncing ball or large-angle pendulum is periodic but not SHM. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A 0.2 kg mass hung on a spring stretches it by 0.04 m at equilibrium. Calculate the spring constant.
A 0.3 kg mass hung on a spring stretches it by 0.05 m at equilibrium. Calculate the spring constant.

A 0.40 kg mass hangs at rest on a spring, extending it by 0.098 m. It is pulled down a further 0.050 m and released. (a) Calculate the spring constant. (b) Show that the motion is SHM and calculate ω. (c) Calculate the maximum acceleration. (d) State the period and explain why it would be the same for a 0.030 m pull.
items.answer: (a) k = mg/x = 40.0 N m⁻¹; (b) F = −kx about equilibrium, so a = −(k/m)x; ω = √(40/0.40) = 10.0 rad s⁻¹; (c) a_max = ω²A = 5.0 m s⁻²; (d) T = 0.628 s; period is independent of amplitude in SHM.
items.markingKey: (a) k = mg/x = 40.0 N m⁻¹; (b) F = −kx about equilibrium, so a = −(k/m)x; ω = √(40/0.40) = 10.0 rad s⁻¹; (c) a_max = ω²A = 5.0 m s⁻²; (d) T = 0.628 s; period is independent of amplitude in SHM.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "isochronous oscillation"?
options: A point mass on a light inextensible string; for small oscillations T = 2π√(L/g)
The quantity ω = 2πf = 2π/T, in rad s⁻¹
The distance and direction of the object from its equilibrium position
An oscillation whose period does not depend on its amplitude, a key feature of SHM
items.answer: An oscillation whose period does not depend on its amplitude, a key feature of SHM
items.markingKey: D. "isochronous oscillation" is an oscillation whose period does not depend on its amplitude, a key feature of SHM.

items.stem: Which of the following statements about conditions for SHM: restoring force proportional to displacement is a common misconception? (Revision quiz set by Mei.)
options: In SHM the velocity is greatest at the extremes of the motion.
ωt is in radians, since ω is in rad s⁻¹; calculators must be in radian mode.
Only oscillations with a ∝ −x are SHM; a bouncing ball or large-angle pendulum is periodic but not SHM.
At x = x₀/2, E_p = ¼E_T and E_k = ¾E_T; they are equal at x = x₀/√2.
items.answer: In SHM the velocity is greatest at the extremes of the motion.
items.markingKey: A. This is incorrect: The velocity is zero at the extremes (turning points) and maximum at equilibrium.

items.stem: Explain the difference between other periodic motion and simple harmonic motion.
items.answer: All periodic motion repeats at regular intervals, but in SHM the acceleration must be proportional to displacement and directed towards equilibrium, giving sinusoidal motion and an amplitude-independent period.
items.markingKey: All periodic motion repeats at regular intervals, but in SHM the acceleration must be proportional to displacement and directed towards equilibrium, giving sinusoidal motion and an amplitude-independent period. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: An oscillator in SHM is at its maximum positive displacement. Its acceleration is
items.answer: maximum and negative
items.markingKey: A. a = −ω²A.

items.stem: An object performs SHM with angular frequency 8.0 rad s⁻¹. Calculate the magnitude of its acceleration when its displacement is 0.1 m.
A 0.1 kg mass is attached to a spring of spring constant 80 N m⁻¹. Calculate the angular frequency of its oscillations.
items.answer: 28.3 rad s⁻¹

items.stem: A student claims: "All oscillations are simple harmonic." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Only oscillations with a ∝ −x are SHM; a bouncing ball or large-angle pendulum is periodic but not SHM.
items.markingKey: Only oscillations with a ∝ −x are SHM; a bouncing ball or large-angle pendulum is periodic but not SHM. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Many real oscillating systems can be treated as simple harmonic."
items.answer: SHM is an excellent first model for small oscillations near equilibrium, but real systems require damping and non-linear terms at larger amplitudes.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: small oscillations about a stable equilibrium are approximately SHM (Taylor expansion); pendulums, springs, molecules in solids, tuning forks. Arguments against: large amplitudes introduce non-linearity; damping and driving forces modify the motion; some systems (bouncing balls) are never SHM. Supported judgement: SHM is an excellent first model for small oscillations near equilibrium, but real systems require damping and non-linear terms at larger amplitudes. Markbands (10 marks): Top band: focused, balanced argument, well-chosen specific evidence, and a reasoned judgement that follows from the analysis.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A point mass on a light inextensible string; for small oscillations T = 2π√(L/g)"?
items.answer: simple pendulum
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of simple pendulum.

items.stem: Tomás and a classmate in Seoul disagree about time period, frequency, amplitude and phase; the mass-spring system and simple pendulum. Which statement is correct?
options: In SHM the period is independent of amplitude.
Displacement and velocity in SHM are in phase.
Doubling the amplitude of an SHM oscillator doubles its period.
items.answer: In SHM the period is independent of amplitude.
items.markingKey: B. The other options are common misconceptions. In SHM the period is independent of amplitude.

items.stem: The mass on a spring is replaced by one four times as heavy. The period
items.answer: doubles
items.markingKey: D. T ∝ √m.

items.stem: Noah timed a pendulum with a hand-held stopwatch, starting at the centre of the swing. The repeated readings of the time for 20 oscillations of a pendulum were 34.4, 34.5, 34.8, 34.5 s. Calculate the mean value and its absolute uncertainty.
items.markingKey: Mean = 34.5 s (A1); uncertainty = half the range = (34.8 − 34.4)/2 = 0.2 s (A1).

items.stem:
The period T of a simple pendulum is measured (by timing 20 oscillations) for different lengths L. Theory: T = 2π√(L/g).

L / m | T / s
0.200 | 0.891
0.400 | 1.269
0.600 | 1.543
0.800 | 1.806
1.000 | 1.996
1.200 | 2.199

(a) State the quantities that should be plotted to obtain a straight line. [1]
(b) Using the data, determine the gradient of the best-fit line. [2]
(c) Hence determine the acceleration of free fall g. [1]
(d) The gradients of the maximum and minimum lines differ from the best-fit gradient by ±4 %. State g with its absolute uncertainty. [1]
items.answer: (a) T² (y) against L (x); (b) gradient ≈ 4.03 s² m⁻¹; (c) 9.80 m s⁻²; (d) (9.8 ± 0.4) m s⁻²
items.markingKey: (a) T² (y) against L (x) (A1). (b) Best-fit line through the plotted points (M1); gradient ≈ 4.03 s² m⁻¹ – accept ±3 % (A1). (c) g = 4π²/gradient = 9.80 m s⁻² (A1). (d) absolute uncertainty = 4 % of the value = 0.4 m s⁻²; value quoted to the same precision (A1).

items.stem: A grandfather clock in Mexico City needs a pendulum with a period of 1.0 s. Calculate the required length.

A student measures the time for 20 swings of a pendulum of length 0.800 m as 35.9 s, with a reaction-time uncertainty of ±0.2 s and length uncertainty ±0.002 m. (a) Calculate T and its uncertainty. (b) Calculate g. (c) Determine the percentage uncertainty in g. (d) Suggest one systematic error and how to reduce it.
items.answer: (a) T = 1.795 ± 0.010 s; (b) g = 4π²L/T² = 9.80 m s⁻²; (c) %g = %L + 2 × %T = 0.25 + 1.1 = 1.4 %; (d) length measured to the top of the bob rather than its centre – measure to the centre or plot T² against L and use the gradient.
items.markingKey: (a) T = 1.795 ± 0.010 s; (b) g = 4π²L/T² = 9.80 m s⁻²; (c) %g = %L + 2 × %T = 0.25 + 1.1 = 1.4 %; (d) length measured to the top of the bob rather than its centre – measure to the centre or plot T² against L and use the gradient.

items.stem:
Masses m are hung from a spring and set oscillating vertically. The period T is found by timing 10 oscillations. Theory: T = 2π√(m/k).

m / kg | T / s
0.100 | 0.486
0.200 | 0.676
0.300 | 0.839
0.400 | 0.970
0.500 | 1.076
0.600 | 1.191

(a) State the quantities that should be plotted to obtain a straight line. [1]
(b) Using the data, determine the gradient of the best-fit line. [2]
(c) Hence determine the spring constant k. [1]
(d) The gradients of the maximum and minimum lines differ from the best-fit gradient by ±4 %. State k with its absolute uncertainty. [1]
items.answer: (a) T² (y) against m (x); (b) gradient ≈ 2.36 s² kg⁻¹; (c) 16.7 N m⁻¹; (d) (16.7 ± 0.7) N m⁻¹
items.markingKey: (a) T² (y) against m (x) (A1). (b) Best-fit line through the plotted points (M1); gradient ≈ 2.36 s² kg⁻¹ – accept ±3 % (A1). (c) k = 4π²/gradient = 16.7 N m⁻¹ (A1). (d) absolute uncertainty = 4 % of the value = 0.7 N m⁻¹; value quoted to the same precision (A1).

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "phase difference"?
options: Oscillatory motion in which the acceleration is proportional to the displacement from a fixed equilibrium point and always directed towards it: a = −ω²x
The sum of kinetic and potential energy, E_T = ½mω²x₀², constant in the absence of damping
The fraction of a cycle (expressed as an angle in radians) by which one oscillation leads or lags another
The distance and direction of the object from its equilibrium position
items.answer: The fraction of a cycle (expressed as an angle in radians) by which one oscillation leads or lags another
items.markingKey: C. "phase difference" is the fraction of a cycle (expressed as an angle in radians) by which one oscillation leads or lags another.

items.stem: Define the term "frequency".
items.answer: The number of oscillations per unit time, f = 1/T, in hertz
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the number of oscillations per unit time, f = 1/T, in hertz. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Distinguish between the simple pendulum and the mass–spring system.
items.answer: For a mass on a spring T = 2π√(m/k), depending on mass and stiffness but not g; for a simple pendulum T = 2π√(L/g), depending on length and g but not on mass.
items.markingKey: For a mass on a spring T = 2π√(m/k), depending on mass and stiffness but not g; for a simple pendulum T = 2π√(L/g), depending on length and g but not on mass. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why a pendulum clock taken to the top of a high mountain runs slow.
items.answer: g is slightly smaller further from Earth’s centre; T = 2π√(L/g) increases, so the clock completes fewer swings per hour and loses time.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: g is slightly smaller further from Earth’s centre; T = 2π√(L/g) increases, so the clock completes fewer swings per hour and loses time. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "Phase difference is measured in seconds." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: It is an angle (rad or degrees) or a fraction of a cycle; a time difference Δt corresponds to a phase difference 2πΔt/T.
items.markingKey: It is an angle (rad or degrees) or a fraction of a cycle; a time difference Δt corresponds to a phase difference 2πΔt/T. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Two pendulums of period 0.4 s swing with one reaching its maximum displacement 0.125 s after the other. Calculate the phase difference in radians.
items.answer: 1.96 rad
items.markingKey: C. Δφ = 2πΔt/T (M1) = 1.96 rad (A1).

items.stem: A student claims: "Phase difference is measured in seconds." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: It is an angle (rad or degrees) or a fraction of a cycle; a time difference Δt corresponds to a phase difference 2πΔt/T.
items.markingKey: It is an angle (rad or degrees) or a fraction of a cycle; a time difference Δt corresponds to a phase difference 2πΔt/T. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A pendulum of length 1.0 m is taken to Venus, where g = 8.87 m s⁻². Calculate its period there.
"Pendulums are no longer useful in science now that atomic clocks exist." Discuss.
items.answer: Pendulums are obsolete for precise timekeeping but remain valuable for measurement, demonstration and as models of oscillation.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: atomic clocks are far more accurate. Arguments against: pendulums are still used to measure g and teach SHM; Foucault pendulums demonstrate Earth’s rotation; gravimeters and seismometers use pendulum principles. Supported judgement: Pendulums are obsolete for precise timekeeping but remain valuable for measurement, demonstration and as models of oscillation. Markbands (10 marks): Top band: focused, balanced argument, well-chosen specific evidence, and a reasoned judgement that follows from the analysis.

items.stem:
This question is about time period, frequency, amplitude and phase; the mass-spring system and simple pendulum.

(a) Maya timed a pendulum with a hand-held stopwatch, starting at the centre of the swing. The 5 readings of the time for 20 oscillations of a pendulum were 36.3, 34.8, 35.8, 34.8, 35.7 s. Determine the mean, the absolute uncertainty and the percentage uncertainty, and state the result to an appropriate number of significant figures. [3]

(b) With the help of a specific example, explain why the period of a mass–spring system does not depend on g, while a pendulum’s does. [3]

(c) "Pendulums are no longer useful in science now that atomic clocks exist." Discuss this view, referring to the physics of time period, frequency, amplitude and phase. [4]
items.answer: (a) 35.5 ± 0.8 s (2.1 %) (b) For the spring the restoring force comes from the spring (k), and gravity only shifts the equilibrium position; for the pendulum the restoring force is a component of the weight, so g appears in T. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (c) Pendulums are obsolete for precise timekeeping but remain valuable for measurement, demonstration and as models of oscillation.
items.markingKey: (a) [3 marks] Mean = 35.5 s (A1); absolute uncertainty = half range = 0.8 s (A1); percentage uncertainty = 0.8/35.5 × 100 = 2.1 % (A1). Result quoted to the same decimal place as the uncertainty. (b) [3 marks] For the spring the restoring force comes from the spring (k), and gravity only shifts the equilibrium position; for the pendulum the restoring force is a component of the weight, so g appears in T. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (c) [4 marks] For: atomic clocks are far more accurate. Against: pendulums are still used to measure g and teach SHM; Foucault pendulums demonstrate Earth’s rotation; gravimeters and seismometers use pendulum principles. Award the final mark(s) for a judgement supported by the arguments: Pendulums are obsolete for precise timekeeping but remain valuable for measurement, demonstration and as models of oscillation.

items.stem: At what displacement is the kinetic energy of an SHM oscillator equal to its potential energy?
items.answer: x = x₀/√2
items.markingKey: x = x₀/√2 (A1). ½x₀² = x².

items.stem: A student in Mexico City is checking notes on energy changes during SHM. Which statement is incorrect?
options: At x = x₀/2, E_p = ¼E_T and E_k = ¾E_T; they are equal at x = x₀/√2.
Velocity leads displacement by π/2: it is maximum when x = 0.
The velocity is zero at the extremes (turning points) and maximum at equilibrium.
A stiffer spring with the same mass and amplitude has the same energy.
items.answer: A stiffer spring with the same mass and amplitude has the same energy.
items.markingKey: D. This is incorrect: E = ½kx₀²; a stiffer spring stores more energy for the same amplitude.

items.stem: Leila writes: "The total energy of an SHM oscillator is greatest at the equilibrium position." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: The total energy is constant; only its division between kinetic and potential energy changes.
items.markingKey: The total energy is constant; only its division between kinetic and potential energy changes. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A 1.0 kg mass oscillates on a spring (k = 400 N m⁻¹) with an amplitude of 0.03 m. Calculate its maximum speed.
items.markingKey: B. ω = √(k/m) = 20.0 rad s⁻¹ (M1); v_max = ωx₀ = 0.600 m s⁻¹ (A1).

items.stem: An oscillator of mass 0.1 kg and angular frequency 14.1 rad s⁻¹ has amplitude 0.03 m. Calculate its kinetic energy when the displacement is 0.0150 m.
items.markingKey: E_k = ½mω²(x₀² − x²) (M1) = 0.00675 J (A1).

items.stem: A 0.50 kg mass on a spring (k = 200 N m⁻¹) oscillates horizontally on a frictionless surface with amplitude 0.060 m. (a) Calculate the total energy. (b) Calculate the maximum speed. (c) Determine the speed and the kinetic energy when x = 0.030 m. (d) Sketch graphs of E_k, E_p and E_T against displacement.
items.answer: (a) E = ½ × 200 × 0.060² = 0.36 J; (b) v_max = ωx₀ = 20 × 0.060 = 1.2 m s⁻¹; (c) v = ω√(x₀² − x²) = 1.04 m s⁻¹, E_k = 0.27 J; (d) inverted parabola for E_k, parabola for E_p, horizontal line for E_T.
items.markingKey: (a) E = ½ × 200 × 0.060² = 0.36 J; (b) v_max = ωx₀ = 20 × 0.060 = 1.2 m s⁻¹; (c) v = ω√(x₀² − x²) = 1.04 m s⁻¹, E_k = 0.27 J; (d) inverted parabola for E_k, parabola for E_p, horizontal line for E_T.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "potential energy in SHM"?
options: The stored energy E_p = ½mω²x², maximum at the extremes of motion
The expression x = x₀ sin(ωt + φ) (or x₀ cos(ωt + φ)), where φ is the phase angle
The number of oscillations per unit time, f = 1/T, in hertz
items.answer: The stored energy E_p = ½mω²x², maximum at the extremes of motion
items.markingKey: A. "potential energy in SHM" is the stored energy E_p = ½mω²x², maximum at the extremes of motion.

items.stem: Briefly explain why the graph of kinetic energy against displacement for an SHM oscillator is a parabola.
items.answer: E_k = ½mω²(x₀² − x²), a quadratic in x, maximum at x = 0 and zero at x = ±x₀.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: E_k = ½mω²(x₀² − x²), a quadratic in x, maximum at x = 0 and zero at x = ±x₀. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A graph of potential energy against displacement for an SHM oscillator is
options: a parabola with minimum at x = 0
items.answer: a parabola with minimum at x = 0
items.markingKey: D. E_p = ½mω²x².

items.stem: Explain the difference between potential energy in SHM and kinetic energy in SHM.
items.answer: Kinetic energy is maximum at equilibrium and zero at the extremes; potential energy is zero at equilibrium and maximum at the extremes; their sum is constant without damping.
items.markingKey: Kinetic energy is maximum at equilibrium and zero at the extremes; potential energy is zero at equilibrium and maximum at the extremes; their sum is constant without damping. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: An SHM oscillator has amplitude 0.08 m. At what displacement is its potential energy 50 % of its total energy?
A 0.5 kg mass oscillates on a spring (k = 20 N m⁻¹) with an amplitude of 0.05 m. Calculate its maximum speed.
items.markingKey: ω = √(k/m) = 6.32 rad s⁻¹ (M1); v_max = ωx₀ = 0.316 m s⁻¹ (A1).

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Energy methods are always the best way to analyse SHM problems."
items.answer: Energy methods are efficient for speed–displacement relationships, while time-based equations are needed for phase and timing.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: give speeds at any displacement quickly; avoid trigonometric functions of time. Arguments against: they give no information about timing or phase; damping and driving forces complicate the energy accounting. Supported judgement: Energy methods are efficient for speed–displacement relationships, while time-based equations are needed for phase and timing. Markbands (10 marks): Top band: focused, balanced argument, well-chosen specific evidence, and a reasoned judgement that follows from the analysis.

items.stem:
This question is about energy changes during SHM.

(a) A pendulum of length 1.0 m is released from rest at 12° to the vertical. Calculate its maximum speed. [2]

(b) Distinguish between potential energy in SHM and kinetic energy in SHM. [4]

(c) "Energy methods are always the best way to analyse SHM problems." Discuss this view, referring to the physics of energy changes during SHM. [6]

(c) Energy methods are efficient for speed–displacement relationships, while time-based equations are needed for phase and timing.

(b) [4 marks] Kinetic energy is maximum at equilibrium and zero at the extremes; potential energy is zero at equilibrium and maximum at the extremes; their sum is constant without damping. items.stem: Define the term "acceleration equation of SHM".
items.answer: The expression a = −ω²x₀ sin(ωt + φ) = −ω²x
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the expression a = −ω²x₀ sin(ωt + φ) = −ω²x. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain how the velocity–time graph of an SHM oscillator can be obtained from its displacement–time graph.
items.answer: Velocity is the gradient of the displacement–time graph; for a sine curve the gradient is a cosine curve of amplitude ωx₀, so the v–t graph is shifted a quarter cycle ahead.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Velocity is the gradient of the displacement–time graph; for a sine curve the gradient is a cosine curve of amplitude ωx₀, so the v–t graph is shifted a quarter cycle ahead. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Which of the following statements about equations of SHM: displacement, velocity and acceleration (HL) is a common misconception? (Revision quiz set by Lars.)
options: In SHM the period is independent of amplitude.
The velocity is zero at the extremes (turning points) and maximum at equilibrium.
In x = x₀ sin ωt, ωt should be calculated in degrees.
Only oscillations with a ∝ −x are SHM; a bouncing ball or large-angle pendulum is periodic but not SHM.
items.answer: In x = x₀ sin ωt, ωt should be calculated in degrees.
items.markingKey: C. This is incorrect: ωt is in radians, since ω is in rad s⁻¹; calculators must be in radian mode.

items.stem: An oscillator passes through equilibrium moving in the positive direction at t = 0 (x = x₀ sin ωt), with x₀ = 0.05 m and f = 2.0 Hz. Calculate its velocity at t = 0.125 s.
"The acceleration of an SHM oscillator is greatest when its speed is greatest." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Acceleration is greatest at the extremes where the speed is zero; at equilibrium speed is maximum and acceleration is zero.
items.markingKey: Acceleration is greatest at the extremes where the speed is zero; at equilibrium speed is maximum and acceleration is zero. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Describing oscillations by sinusoidal equations is just a mathematical convenience."
items.answer: Sinusoidal descriptions follow directly from the physics of linear restoring forces and are confirmed by measurement, making them much more than a convenience.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: sin/cos solve a = −ω²x exactly. Arguments against: the same mathematics describes AC circuits, waves, quantum oscillators; Fourier analysis shows any periodic motion can be built from sinusoids; measurements of real oscillators match the predicted waveforms. Supported judgement: Sinusoidal descriptions follow directly from the physics of linear restoring forces and are confirmed by measurement, making them much more than a convenience.

items.stem: The maximum acceleration of an oscillator is
items.answer: ω²x₀
items.markingKey: D. a = −ω²x.

items.stem: Distinguish between x = x₀ sin ωt and x = x₀ cos ωt.
items.answer: Both describe SHM with the same ω and amplitude; sin starts at equilibrium moving in the positive direction at t = 0, cos starts at maximum displacement at rest. They differ by a phase of π/2.
items.markingKey: Both describe SHM with the same ω and amplitude; sin starts at equilibrium moving in the positive direction at t = 0, cos starts at maximum displacement at rest. They differ by a phase of π/2. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the significance of the negative sign in a = −ω²x.
items.answer: It shows the acceleration is always directed opposite to the displacement, i.e. towards the equilibrium position (restoring).
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It shows the acceleration is always directed opposite to the displacement, i.e. towards the equilibrium position (restoring). (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A loudspeaker cone vibrates in SHM at 400 Hz with amplitude 0.0008 m. Calculate its maximum acceleration.
An oscillator starts at maximum displacement x₀ at t = 0 and oscillates at 2.5 Hz. Calculate the first time at which its displacement is 0.5 x₀.
"Displacement and velocity in SHM are in phase." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Velocity leads displacement by π/2: it is maximum when x = 0.
items.markingKey: Velocity leads displacement by π/2: it is maximum when x = 0. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A piston in a model engine moves with approximately SHM of amplitude 0.040 m and frequency 25 Hz. (a) Calculate ω. (b) Calculate the maximum speed and maximum acceleration of the piston. (c) Write an equation for x(t), taking x = +0.040 m at t = 0. (d) Calculate the displacement and velocity at t = 0.0050 s.

This question is about equations of SHM: displacement, velocity and acceleration (HL).

(a) An oscillator passes through equilibrium moving in the positive direction at t = 0 (x = x₀ sin ωt), with x₀ = 0.05 m and f = 2.5 Hz. Calculate its velocity at t = 0.2 s. [2]

(b) With the help of a specific example, explain how the velocity–time graph of an SHM oscillator can be obtained from its displacement–time graph. [3]

(c) "Describing oscillations by sinusoidal equations is just a mathematical convenience." Discuss this view, referring to the physics of equations of SHM. [6]
items.answer: (a) −0.785 m s⁻¹ (b) Velocity is the gradient of the displacement–time graph; for a sine curve the gradient is a cosine curve of amplitude ωx₀, so the v–t graph is shifted a quarter cycle ahead. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (c) Sinusoidal descriptions follow directly from the physics of linear restoring forces and are confirmed by measurement, making them much more than a convenience.

Against: the same mathematics describes AC circuits, waves, quantum oscillators; Fourier analysis shows any periodic motion can be built from sinusoids; measurements of real oscillators match the predicted waveforms. Award the final mark(s) for a judgement supported by the arguments: Sinusoidal descriptions follow directly from the physics of linear restoring forces and are confirmed by measurement, making them much more than a convenience.

items.answer: (a) 0.450 m s⁻² (b) All periodic motion repeats at regular intervals, but in SHM the acceleration must be proportional to displacement and directed towards equilibrium, giving sinusoidal motion and an amplitude-independent period. (c) SHM is an excellent first model for small oscillations near equilibrium, but real systems require damping and non-linear terms at larger amplitudes.

(c) [4 marks] For: small oscillations about a stable equilibrium are approximately SHM (Taylor expansion); pendulums, springs, molecules in solids, tuning forks. Against: large amplitudes introduce non-linearity; damping and driving forces modify the motion; some systems (bouncing balls) are never SHM. Award the final mark(s) for a judgement supported by the arguments: SHM is an excellent first model for small oscillations near equilibrium, but real systems require damping and non-linear terms at larger amplitudes.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "period"?

The time for one complete oscillation, T
The quantity ω = 2πf = 2π/T, in rad s⁻¹

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "damping".

items.stem: Explain the difference between x = x₀ sin ωt and x = x₀ cos ωt.
items.answer: Both describe SHM with the same ω and amplitude; sin starts at equilibrium moving in the positive direction at t = 0, cos starts at maximum displacement at rest. They differ by a phase of π/2.

items.stem: Which of the following statements about time period, frequency, amplitude and phase; the mass-spring system and simple pendulum is a common misconception? (Revision quiz set by Kwame.)
options: The total energy is constant; only its division between kinetic and potential energy changes.
E = ½kx₀²; a stiffer spring stores more energy for the same amplitude.
Only oscillations with a ∝ −x are SHM; a bouncing ball or large-angle pendulum is periodic but not SHM.
A heavier pendulum bob swings more slowly.
items.answer: A heavier pendulum bob swings more slowly.
items.markingKey: D. This is incorrect: The period of a simple pendulum is independent of mass: both the restoring force and the inertia scale with m.

items.stem: Briefly explain why a simple pendulum only approximates SHM for small amplitudes.
items.answer: The restoring force is −mg sin θ; only for small θ is sin θ ≈ θ ≈ x/L, giving a = −(g/L)x. For large angles the force is no longer proportional to displacement.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The restoring force is −mg sin θ; only for small θ is sin θ ≈ θ ≈ x/L, giving a = −(g/L)x. For large angles the force is no longer proportional to displacement. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

ωt is in radians, since ω is in rad s⁻¹; calculators must be in radian mode.

items.markingKey: D. This is incorrect: Acceleration is greatest at the extremes where the speed is zero; at equilibrium speed is maximum and acceleration is zero.

items.answer: The human reaction-time uncertainty (~0.2 s) is a fixed absolute error; spreading it over 20 periods reduces the percentage uncertainty in T by a factor of 20.
